lesson.title: Legislating Neutrality: The Acts That Tried to Keep America Out of War
lesson.summary: Between 1935 and 1939, Congress passed a series of Neutrality Acts meant to prevent the kind of entanglements that had drawn the United States into World War One, only to loosen those restrictions as the threat from fascist aggression grew.
lesson.body:
Rooted in the isolationist conviction that arms sales and loans to warring nations had helped pull the United States into World War One, and reinforced by the Nye Committee's findings on wartime profiteering, Congress moved to legally bar such entanglements before they could happen again.

The Neutrality Act of 1935 imposed an automatic arms embargo on all belligerents once the president declared that a state of war existed, treating aggressor and victim identically, and it warned American citizens against traveling on ships belonging to nations at war.

The Neutrality Acts of 1936 and 1937 extended these restrictions and added a ban on loans to belligerent nations. The 1937 act also introduced a cash and carry option: belligerents could purchase non military goods from the United States as long as they paid in cash immediately and transported the goods themselves, which reduced the risk that American ships or loans would be dragged into the conflict.

Everything shifted after Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 started the war in Europe. Roosevelt pushed Congress to revise the law, and the Neutrality Act of 1939 lifted the arms embargo entirely and extended cash and carry purchases to weapons as well as other goods. Because Britain and France controlled the Atlantic shipping lanes, this change effectively favored the Allies while still keeping American ships and citizens out of officially declared war zones. It was the first step in a gradual loosening of American neutrality that would continue with measures like the Lend-Lease Act.
